# **~~Monthly Copper Briefing Report~~** 

## **June 2012** 







#### Prices Consolidate Lower 

LME Cash falls by over $500/t 

Cash to 3-month backwarda-on collapsing Output numbers below expecta-on Copper use numbers disappoint even more 

##### Projects re-assessed on lower price outlook 

Not only has the LME Cash price fallen by more than $500/t to range around $7,700/t this month, the mood of the market had changed drama-cally. With the apparent -ghtness in physical copper in April, resul-ng from the concentra-on of available stock in China and a strong holding of LME stock, there had been good reason for copper prices to remain high. The Cash to 3- month backwarda-on was symptoma-c of the market tone. In May, however, the backwarda-on has all but dissipated. As stocks relocate out of China, there is no longer a dominant stock holder on the LME and shorts, that had been scared off by the backwarda-on, begin to re-enter the scene, the copper market of today looks very different from a month ago. Despite the entry of shorts, open interest on the LME has fallen to much lower levels. This results from long liquida-on, reflec-ng a growing consensus that lower prices are here to stay. 

The fall in prices occurred earlier than we had expected. We had been of the view that engineered -ghtness in copper would merge seamlessly into real -ghtness as consump-on picked up to absorb surplus copper. In terms of developments in the demand / supply balance and overall liquid stock change, we weren’t so far wrong. What we hadn’t calculated on was the speed at which stocks would start to relocate out of China (from bonded warehouses and from smelters), nor the early collapse of the dominant stock holder - backwarda-on structure on the LME. 

Looking at the underlying market fundamentals alone, we s-ll have some reason to be op-mis-c. In May, exchange stocks have fallen by 80 kt, and Chinese merchant bonded stocks by at least this amount to reach around 550kt. Also, excess stocks at Chinese smelters have fallen. Thus, while there is s-ll more liquid stock in China than is comfortable, there is not very much at all in much of the rest of the world, especially Europe, where LME inventory has fallen to less than 20 kt. 

Going forward, though, a lack of dynamicism in China and a feed-through of the Eurozone crisis to the real economy gives us less hope that consump-on will pick up much in coming months, Copper use is almost certain 



to struggle to keep up with growing copper output. The struggle would already be greater had not copper output con-nued to come in below expecta-on.. 

A wide acceptance of a more nega-ve forward view is really the over-riding theme right now for copper, as for other metals. The confident asser-on un-l recently by mining companies that China will con-nue to deliver huge annual increments to metals demand has been replaced by a much more cau-ous stance. ### Prices, Market Balance and Stocks 

##### Copper Prices Track Lower 

From early May, when LME Cash had comfortably regained a price tag of around $8,500/t, prices started to fall. The slide was quite rapid, over the first two weeks of the month taking LME Cash down to a new level in the region of $7,700/t., where it is now placed. In the past week, even quite bullish news including the promise of an RMB 2 billion s-mulus package in China and a temporary stoppage at Collahuasi, has failed to li- prices by that much. Lower prices in part reflect a strengthening US Dollar, but only in part. 

As for forward prices, the LME Cash to three-month backwarda-on that has been such a feature of the copper market  for more than two months has started to collapse. Whereas the spread was over $100/t at the start of May, it is now around $30/t and falling. 

With lower London prices, the gap in pricing with Shanghai has widened. Domes-c Chinese SHFE onemonth prices are now aroun

d 15% higher than LME Cash, compared to just over 10% at the start of May. Although this is not sufficient to allow a pure arbitrage trade, including duty and related costs, the effec-ve gap is now less than $100/t rather than over $500/t. ##### Visible Stocks Fall and Relocate While prices have been falling, the physical market has started to look -ghter. In May so far, total exchange stocks have fallen by 80 kt. The biggest reduc-on, of 48 kt, has been on the SHFE. Comex also has seen a drop while, a-er a 20 kt fall in the first two weeks of the month, total LME stocks have been more-or-less sta-c at around 225 kt. The net movement of stock on the LME has been quite small, but the loca-on of stock has changed quite drama-cally. The United States has seen a sharp drawdown of around 25 kt. More important, a slightly smaller shi- out of Europe has le- the region’s LME stock at less than 20 kt, a very low level indeed. In contrast, Asian stocks in Korea and Singapore have seen a big increase. The rise in Asian LME stock reflects movement out of China. With a nearby backwarda-on making holding metal less a-rac-ve and rela-vely low SHFE prices discouraging domes-c deliveries, Chinese merchant bonded copper has been released on to the LME. In both March and April, China exported over 25 kt of refined copper. This is unusual, as China rarely exports much cathode. It seems, however, that the export volume from China is rising, and more from the smelters than the bonded warehouses. pying and Electronic Forwarding Prohibited Email: reports@intierra.com** ### Macroeconomic Trends The odds that Greece exits the Euro have been drama-cally increased in the past weeks as the frontrunning poli-cal par-es were unable, or unwilling, to form a coali-on government a-er the divisive result of May elec-ons. New elec-ons are planned for June 17th, but hopes for a las-ng Greek solu-on are diminishing. Now, European officials quite openly acknowledge they are working on a con-ngency plan for a “Grexit”; Chris-ne Lagarde says the IMF is considering this too. It seems that the ques-on is not anymore if, but when, and how. Especially the “how”, as this has deep implica-ons for what happens next in the other troubled countries of southern Europe. With US$1.2 trillion in Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and Irish debt, Europe’s lenders s-ll face deposit flight risk and rising defaults elsewhere. Many fear a domino effect following a Greek exit, with a call on bail out funds that simply cannot, or will not, be met. Global IP rose by an es-mated 0.2% on a month-onmonth basis in March a-er rising by 0.3% in February. OECD produc-on fell by 0.2% while non-OECD output was up by 0.7%. While Chinese IP growth was down, flash PMI for May suggest that there may be more to come. The index fell to 48.7 in May from a final reading of 49.3 in April, stoking fears that the Chinese economy could slow sharply. IP Development in Selected Countries

As for China, recent economic data shows further slowdown, especially in middle-market manufacturing, indica-ng that problems in China’s export industries may be turning structural. Also, latest trade balance figures show slowing imports, when normal seasonal pa-erns suggest an increase. ### Consump-on Trends The Chinese government is looking for ways to bring forward the start up of infrastructure projects that had been originally planned to commence in 2013. This is to counter weak economic growth. That, in combina-on with the new subsidies for energy efficient consumer goods announced in May, is expected to have posi-ve impact on the demand for copper products. However, there is li-le sign yet in the order books that the restraint in copper use will improve much in coming months. Demand for copper tubes remains slow as sales of air condi-oners is s-ll down on last year, although not by as much as the 8% year-on-year drop in January-February. Power cable figures are more posi-ve, with output up by 11% year-on-year in Q1 2012. This market is expected to strengthen as a result of increased spending by the power u-li-es. As the major fabricators publish their Q1 financials, the consump-on trends so far and expecta-ons for the remainder of this year become clearer. Cable producer Prysmian expects glob

al demand for medium voltage cables for u-li-es and for building wire to remain stable in the next months, with be-er prospects in submarine, offshore oil and gas and renewable energy markets. Meanwhile, copper/alloy mill products company KME, which suffered a 15% output decline for its semi-finished, copper alloy and special products in the first quarter, predicts that the weak demand from the construc-on industry will con-nue. Certainly, this appears to be the case over much of Europe. As for the automo-ve sector, German harness producer Leoni, sees substan-al growth, especially in the United States and the emerging geographies, offse-ng a weaker market in Europe. ##### Appe-te for Mine Investment Lower The mining industry is entering into a new era as the “supercycle” in commodity prices, driven in part by China’s rapid infrastructure build out, appears to be coming to a close. BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto have acknowledged the sea change, and have announced plans to re-evaluate their development por-olio. Casual-es for copper were almost immediate. BHP quit a small joint venture to define the Al-a copper-silver prospect in Queensland, Australia just a day a-er the company's leadership warned it would cut back on spendi

ng. On a much larger scale, BHP is likely to revise its hugely ambi-ous US$30 billion expansion of Olympic Dam. Whether or not the 750 ktpy project is the next in line to be postponed, delayed, downsized or even cancelled will be decided in June. But, the point is, the cancella-on of such large projects has now entered into the realm of the possible. The prospect of lower than expected demand growth and falling prices bring into focus a number of issues that, un-l now, haven’t really affected future investment plans that much. Now these issues really ma-er. One is the sharp re-evalua-on of capital costs for many planned projects. Rio Tinto now es-mates that Oyu Tolgoi in Mongolia will cost US$13.2 billion instead of the US$9.55 billion es-mated earlier. Project financing, too, has become more of a headache. Having decided to go alone on the Cobre Panama project, Inmet is faced with having to finance US$6.2 billion development, up from the previously es-mated US$4.3 billion. To do this, it plans to raise US$1 billion with a senior unsecured note offering and is considering a further US$1 billion in a precious metals stream financing deal. Not only do even the larger companies have to be more innova-ve in financing, the process is also becoming less certain. CNMC, currently targe-ng to raise capital through the sale of shares on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange to finance Zambian developments, has adjusted its ambi-ons, expec-ng to raise US$313 million rather than the originally planned US$500 million. Add to this par-al withdrawal from projects such as Tia Maria and Congo in Peru where environmental objec-ons hold huge risks, uncertain permi-ng by government in countries such as Indonesia and the Philippines and increased government take in taxes, and it seems that developments that not so long ago were certain are no longer so. Indonesia: The Indonesian government has started to implement a 20% export duty on 21 metal ore and concentrates products, including copper, under new regula-ons applied from May 6th. The government aims to boost investment in domes-c ore processing and to li- exports of higher value finished metals. Energy and Minerals Minister Jero Wacik said that the regula-on "will not allow anyone to export raw material, unless they submi-ed a roadmap to build a smelter". Up to now, the ministry has received 82 proposals for smel-ng projects out of the 400 mining firms working in Indonesia. In addi-on, the government intends to implement export quotas between June and August, the amount allowed for each firm being based on 2009 or 2010 export performance. The new rules do not apply to companies such as Freeport-McMoRan, Vale Indonesia and Newmont Corp., which hold decades-long Contracts of Work (COW), although the government has indicated that it wishes to renego-ate even these agreements. Baiyin Nonferrous Metals Co., Ltd. completed a copper smelter furnace converter technology upgrade in February 2012.
